claim: CHARGE syndrome is caused by heterozygous mutations in the chromatin remodeler, CHD7.
source: CHARGE syndrome is caused by heterozygous mutations in the chromatin remodeler, CHD7, and is characterized by a set of malformations that, on clinical grounds, were historically postulated to arise from defects in neural crest formation during embryogenesis.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the citation of Vissers et al., 2004 in the Introduction.

claim: CHARGE syndrome is characterized by a set of malformations that were historically postulated to arise from defects in neural crest formation during embryogenesis.
source: CHARGE syndrome is caused by heterozygous mutations in the chromatin remodeler, CHD7, and is characterized by a set of malformations that, on clinical grounds, were historically postulated to arise from defects in neural crest formation during embryogenesis.
evidence: This is a historical inference mentioned in the abstract and supported by citations in the Introduction (Siebert et al., 1985).

claim: Expression of genes associated with cell migration was altered in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs compared to control iPSC-NCCs.
source: We found that expression of genes associated with cell migration was altered in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs compared to control iPSC-NCCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray data presented in Figure 3 and qRT-PCR validation in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CHARGE iPSC-NCCs showed defective delamination in vitro.
source: Consistently, CHARGE iPSC-NCCs showed defective delamination, migration and motility in vitro, and their transplantation in ovo revealed overall defective migratory activity in the chick embryo.
evidence: This is supported by the scattering assay data shown in Figure 4, including Delaunay triangulation analysis and intercellular contact quantification.

claim: CHARGE iPSC-NCCs showed defective migration in vitro.
source: Consistently, CHARGE iPSC-NCCs showed defective delamination, migration and motility in vitro, and their transplantation in ovo revealed overall defective migratory activity in the chick embryo.
evidence: This is supported by xCELLigence transwell migration assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: CHARGE iPSC-NCCs showed defective motility in vitro.
source: Consistently, CHARGE iPSC-NCCs showed defective delamination, migration and motility in vitro, and their transplantation in ovo revealed overall defective migratory activity in the chick embryo.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse analysis of spontaneous single cell motility shown in Figure 6.

claim: Transplantation of CHARGE iPSC-NCCs in ovo revealed overall defective migratory activity in the chick embryo.
source: Consistently, CHARGE iPSC-NCCs showed defective delamination, migration and motility in vitro, and their transplantation in ovo revealed overall defective migratory activity in the chick embryo.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo transplantation experiments in chick embryos shown in Figure 7.

claim: This study provides the first successful application of patient-derived iPSCs in modeling craniofacial disorders.
source: These results support the historical inference that CHARGE syndrome patients exhibit defects in neural crest migration, and provide the first successful application of patient-derived iPSCs in modeling craniofacial disorders.
evidence: This is a claim made by the authors about the novelty of their work.

claim: CHARGE syndrome occurs approximately one in 10,000 births.
source: This syndrome is relatively common, occurring approximately one in 10,000 births.
evidence: This is a known epidemiological fact about CHARGE syndrome.

claim: De novo mutations in CHD7 (chromodomain helicase DNA binding protein 7) might be the cause of CHARGE syndrome.
source: Since the first report that de novo mutations in CHD7 (chromodomain helicase DNA binding protein 7) might be the cause of CHARGE syndrome (Vissers et al., 2004), several groups have sought to identify genotype-phenotype correlations and to determine how various phenotypic features of CHARGE are contributed to by CHD7 mutations (Aramaki et al., 2006a; Sanlaville et al., 2006; Zentner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the citation of Vissers et al., 2004.

claim: CHD7 is expressed in various cell types, including pluripotent stem cells and cells of the neural tube and placodal regions.
source: CHD7 is expressed in various cell types, including pluripotent stem cells and cells of the neural tube and placodal regions (Aramaki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the citation of Aramaki et al., 2007.

claim: CHD7 modulates chromatin formation by binding to genomic DNA and regulating the expression of downstream genes.
source: CHD7 modulates chromatin formation by binding to genomic DNA and regulating the expression of downstream genes (Martin, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the citation of Martin, 2010.

claim: Several transcriptional factors, such as SOX2, SOX9, and SOX10, have been reported to cooperate with CHD7 in regulating early development in various cell types.
source: For instance, several transcriptional factors, such as SOX2, SOX9, and SOX10, have been reported to cooperate with CHD7 in regulating early development in various cell types (Bajpai et al., 2010) (He et al., 2016) (Jones et al., 2015) (Micucci et al., 2014) (Schnetz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations: Bajpai et al., 2010; He et al., 2016; Jones et al., 2015; Micucci et al., 2014; Schnetz et al., 2010.

claim: The hypothesis that clinical features observed in CHARGE syndrome patients are caused by abnormalities in neural crest development has been proposed for more than 30 years.
source: The hypothesis that clinical features observed in CHARGE syndrome patients are caused by abnormalities in neural crest development has been proposed for more than 30 years (Siebert et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by the citation of Siebert et al., 1985.

claim: The cells of the neural crest contribute to many different tissue lineages, including those of the craniofacial skeleton, cranial nerves (VII, VIII, IX and X), ears, eyes, and heart.
source: The cells of the neural crest contribute to many different tissue lineages, including those of the craniofacial skeleton, cranial nerves (VII, VIII, IX and X), ears, eyes, and heart.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neural crest cell biology.

claim: CHARGE syndrome is considered as a 'neurocristopathy'.
source: Since many of the defects observed in CHARGE syndrome appear to be related to abnormalities of cranial neural crest cells, this syndrome is considered as a 'neurocristopathy' (Aramaki et al., 2007; Sanlaville et al., 2006; Siebert et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations: Aramaki et al., 2007; Sanlaville et al., 2006; Siebert et al., 1985.

claim: Knockdown of CHD7 in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) results in migratory neural crest formation defects.
source: A recent study supports this view by showing that the knockdown of CHD7 in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) results in migratory neural crest formation defects (Bajpai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the citation of Bajpai et al., 2010.

claim: Knockdown of Chd7 in Xenopus laevis or zebrafish embryos led to abnormalities in neural crest specification and migration.
source: Moreover, the knockdown of Chd7 in Xenopus laevis or zebrafish embryos led to abnormalities in neural crest specification and migration (Asad et al., 2016) (Bajpai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations: Asad et al., 2016; Bajpai et al., 2010.

claim: Both enrolled CHARGE patients have a heterozygous nonsense mutation in CHD7.
source: Both patients have a heterozygous nonsense mutation in CHD7, and exhibited the typical phenotype of CHARGE syndrome (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1D and clinical descriptions in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Both enrolled CHARGE patients exhibited the typical phenotype of CHARGE syndrome.
source: Both patients have a heterozygous nonsense mutation in CHD7, and exhibited the typical phenotype of CHARGE syndrome (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by clinical descriptions provided in Figure 1—source data 1 and the Materials and methods section.

claim: 25 iPSC clones were generated from patient CH1.
source: We collected fibroblasts from these patients and generated 25 and 23 iPSC clones from CH1 and CH2, respectively, following the four-factor protocol first reported by Takahashi and Yamanaka (Takahashi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: 23 iPSC clones were generated from patient CH2.
source: We collected fibroblasts from these patients and generated 25 and 23 iPSC clones from CH1 and CH2, respectively, following the four-factor protocol first reported by Takahashi and Yamanaka (Takahashi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: The generated iPSC clones showed characteristics of pluripotent stem cells, including a morphology similar to that of human embryonic stem cells (ESCs).
source: As shown in Figure 1A–C, these iPSC clones showed characteristics of pluripotent stem cells, including a morphology similar to that of human embryonic stem cells (ESCs) (Figure 1A), the expression of pluripotent stem cell markers (TRA1-60 and TRA1-81) (Figure 1B), and the capacity for teratoma formation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1A.

claim: The generated iPSC clones showed the expression of pluripotent stem cell markers (TRA1-60 and TRA1-81).
source: As shown in Figure 1A–C, these iPSC clones showed characteristics of pluripotent stem cells, including a morphology similar to that of human embryonic stem cells (ESCs) (Figure 1A), the expression of pluripotent stem cell markers (TRA1-60 and TRA1-81) (Figure 1B), and the capacity for teratoma formation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1B.

claim: The generated iPSC clones showed the capacity for teratoma formation.
source: As shown in Figure 1A–C, these iPSC clones showed characteristics of pluripotent stem cells, including a morphology similar to that of human embryonic stem cells (ESCs) (Figure 1A), the expression of pluripotent stem cell markers (TRA1-60 and TRA1-81) (Figure 1B), and the capacity for teratoma formation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis in Figure 1C.

claim: CH1-iPSCs and CH2-iPSCs retained the CHD7 mutations observed in the human dermal fibroblasts (HDFs) of origin.
source: We confirmed that the CH1-iPSCs and CH2-iPSCs retained the CHD7 mutations observed in the human dermal fibroblasts (HDFs) of origin, whereas none of the control iPSCs harbored mutations in CHD7 (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: None of the control iPSCs harbored mutations in CHD7.
source: We confirmed that the CH1-iPSCs and CH2-iPSCs retained the CHD7 mutations observed in the human dermal fibroblasts (HDFs) of origin, whereas none of the control iPSCs harbored mutations in CHD7 (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression levels of CHD7 mRNA in the iPSCs derived from both patients were significantly lower than those in control iPSCs.
source: Interestingly, the expression levels of CHD7 mRNA in the iPSCs derived from both patients were significantly lower than those in control iPSCs (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Neural crest cells are thought to be the primary cells affected in CHARGE syndrome.
source: Neural crest cells are thought to be the primary cells affected in CHARGE syndrome (Blake and Prasad, 2006) (Sanlaville et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations: Blake and Prasad, 2006; Sanlaville et al., 2006.

claim: More than 90% of the cells obtained using Methods A and B from control and CHARGE iPSCs expressed both CD271 and CD57.
source: As shown in Figure 2C and F, more than 90% of the cells obtained using these two methods from control and CHARGE iPSCs expressed both CD271 and CD57.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C and F.

claim: The ratio of CD271 (+) CD57 (+) cells per total induced cells from CHARGE iPSCs was same as that of control without regard to the NCC differentiation method.
source: The ratio of CD271 (+) CD57 (+) cells per total induced cells from CHARGE iPSCs was same as that of control without regard to the NCC differentiation method.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C and F.

claim: iPSC-NCCs expressed neural crest markers including SOX10 and AP2a.
source: We additionally performed an immuno-cytochemical analysis using additional NCCs markers, including SOX10 and AP2a, and we found that the iPSC-NCCs expressed these neural crest markers similarly (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemical data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The NCC differentiation efficacy of CHARGE iPSCs was similar to that of control iPSCs.
source: These results indicate that iPSCs can be differentiated into NCCs, and that the NCC differentiation efficacy of CHARGE iPSCs was similar to that of control iPSCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the flow cytometry and immunocytochemical data showing similar marker expression.

claim: OTX2 was expressed in both control and CHARGE iPSC-NCCs.
source: We determined that OTX2 was expressed in both control and CHARGE iPSC-NCCs (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemical data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: CHARGE iPSC-NCCs can be differentiated into adipocytes, chondrocytes, osteocytes, myofibroblasts, and peripheral neurons.
source: Moreover, using ad hoc protocols, we were able to differentiate CHARGE iPSC-NCCs into adipocytes, chondrocytes, osteocytes, myofibroblasts, and peripheral neurons (Figure 2I, J and K), indicating that these cells exhibit a potential for differentiation similar to control iPSC-NCCs (Bajpai et al., 2010) (Lee and Studer, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by differentiation assays shown in Figure 2I, J and K.

claim: Mutations in CHD7 do not affect NCC differentiation per se.
source: This suggests that mutations in CHD7 do not affect NCC differentiation per se.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CHARGE iPSC-NCCs can differentiate into various cell types similar to control cells.

claim: Control and CHARGE iPSC-NCCs expressed essentially similar profiles of marker gene sets for early (NGFR, B3GAT1, ITGA4), premigratory (PAX3, ZIC1), and migratory (TWIST1) NCCs.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, we found that control and CHARGE iPSC-NCCs expressed essentially similar profiles of marker gene sets for early (NGFR, B3GAT1, ITGA4), premigratory (PAX3, ZIC1), and migratory (TWIST1) NCCs, suggesting the acquisition of the fundamental NCC gene expression profile in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 338 differentially expressed genes (238 upregulated and 100 downregulated in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs) were identified between control and CHARGE iPSC-NCCs (fold change [FC]>1.25).
source: We next extracted 338 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (238 upregulated and 100 downregulated in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs) between control and CHARGE iPSC-NCCs (fold change [FC]>1.25) in an effort to identify features common to genes with altered expression in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by microarray analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of the 338 differentially expressed genes showed enrichment for genes involved in vasculature development, blood vessel development, and blood vessel morphogenesis.
source: A Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of this set showed enrichment for genes involved in vasculature development (p=2.08E-11), blood vessel development (p=1.24E-11), and blood vessel morphogenesis (p=1.23E-09).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis results presented in the text and Figure 3C.

claim: GO terms associated with 'cell migration' and 'cell motion' were significantly enriched in the 338 differentially expressed genes.
source: Interestingly, GO terms associated with 'cell migration' and 'cell motion' were also significantly enriched in these genes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 56 genes under the GO terms 'migration' or 'adhesion' were differentially expressed between control and CHARGE iPSC-NCCs.
source: As shown in Figures 3D, E 56 genes under the GO terms 'migration' or 'adhesion' were differentially expressed.
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figures 3D and E.

claim: Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) analyses confirmed that the changes in POU3F2, OLFM3, CTGF and EDN1 expression observed in the microarray data set were significant.
source: Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) analyses performed for four selected genes, POU3F2, OLFM3, CTGF and EDN1, confirmed that the changes observed in the microarray data set were indeed significant, thereby providing a validation of the analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Direct binding of CHD7 to the distal promoter region in EDN1 was found by ChIP-qPCR.
source: We also performed chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-qPCR for CHD7 using promoter primers for the genes to reveal direct CHD7 binding to these genes, and we found the direct binding of CHD7 to the distal promoter region in EDN1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Control iPSC-NCCs residing at the outermost periphery began to scatter apart in Phase 2.
source: The control iPSC-NCCs residing at the outermost periphery then began to scatter apart (Phase 2) (Figure 4A–a).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 4A-a.

claim: CHARGE iPSC-NCCs exhibited a distinct behavior in Phase 2, remaining closely associated with their neighbors.
source: In contrast, CHARGE iPSC-NCCs exhibited a distinct behavior in Phase 2, remaining closely associated with their neighbors (Figure 4A–b).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 4A-b.

claim: The distribution of the formed triangular area by the Delaunay triangulation algorithm at 8 hr after the sphere attached to the plate was significantly increased relative to that at t = 0 for both control and CHARGE iPSC-NCCs.
source: The distribution of the formed triangular area by the algorithm at 8 hr after the sphere attached to the plate was significantly increased relative to that at t = 0 for both control and CHARGE iPSC-NCCs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by Delaunay triangulation analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Analysis of differences in the increased cell dispersion (from t = 0 to t = 8 hr) revealed a delayed dispersion of cells from CHARGE spheres.
source: Next, we analyzed differences in the increased cell dispersion (from t = 0 to t = 8 hr) between control and CHARGE cells by calculating the median size of the triangular area. We revealed a delayed dispersion of cells from CHARGE spheres (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Quantitative analysis of the number of intercellular contacts among the outermost migrating cells revealed significantly persistent intercellular contacts in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs in vitro.
source: Quantitative analysis of the number of intercellular contacts among the outermost migrating cells revealed significantly persistent intercellular contacts in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs in vitro (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: CHARGE NCCs were reluctant to disperse as single cells, in contrast with control NCCs.
source: CHARGE NCCs were reluctant to disperse as single cells, in contrast with control NCCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the intercellular contact analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: NCC delamination from the neural tube may be affected in CHARGE syndrome.
source: This suggests that NCC delamination from the neural tube may be affected in CHARGE syndrome.
evidence: This is inferred from the scattering assay results showing defective dispersion of CHARGE iPSC-NCCs.

claim: The migration index of CHARGE iPSC-NCCs became lower than that of control cells after approximately 8 hr of monitoring in the xCELLigence assay.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, the migration index of CHARGE iPSC-NCCs became lower than that of control cells after approximately 8 hr of monitoring.
evidence: This is supported by xCELLigence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At 20 hr, there was a decrease of approximately 50% in the migration index of the CHARGE iPSC-NCCs compared with that of control cells.
source: At 20 hr, we observed a decrease of approximately 50% in the migration index of the CHARGE iPSC-NCCs compared with that of control cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by xCELLigence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Aphidicolin treatment did not have a significant effect on the migration index of iPSC-NCCs.
source: To exclude the possibility that the reduction in the number of migrating CHARGE iPSC-NCCs was due to reduced proliferation, we treated control iPSC-NCCs with an antimitotic, aphidicolin. Aphidicolin treatment did not have a significant effect on the migration index of iPSC-NCCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by xCELLigence data with aphidicolin treatment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The proliferative capacity of CHARGE iPSC-NCCs was not different from that of control iPSC-NCCs.
source: Moreover, a BrdU incorporation assay indicated that the proliferative capacity of CHARGE iPSC-NCCs was not different from that of control iPSC-NCCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There was no differential adherence to fibronectin between control and CHARGE iPSC-NCCs.
source: Additionally, to exclude the possibility that lower CHARGE iPSC-NCC adherence to fibronectin caused the reduction in the number of migrating CHARGE iPSC-NCCs in this assay, we performed a cell adhesion assay to fibronectin; we found no differential adherence to fibronectin between control and CHARGE iPSC-NCCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by cell adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CHARGE iPSC-NCCs exhibit aberrant migration, in contrast with their preserved capacity for proliferation and adherence to fibronectin.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that CHARGE iPSC-NCCs exhibit aberrant migration, in contrast with their preserved capacity for proliferation and adherence to fibronectin.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of xCELLigence, BrdU, and adhesion assay results.

claim: At any time interval, the average velocity of the CHARGE iPSC-NCCs (CH1#25) was lower than that of control iPSC-NCCs (201B7).
source: Notably, at any time interval, the average velocity of the CHARGE iPSC-NCCs was lower than that of control iPSC-NCCs (Sidak's multiple comparisons test after two-way repeated measures ANOVA: pTime <0.001, pCellType <0.001; 201B7, N = 80 cells tracked; CH1#25, N = 97 cells tracked).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse tracking data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The directionality of the iPSC-NCCs was constant over time and was similar for both control and CHARGE iPSC-NCCs.
source: In contrast, the directionality of the iPSC-NCCs was constant over time and was similar for both control and CHARGE iPSC-NCCs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by directionality analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The average velocity of CHARGE iPSC-NCCs (CH2#16) migrating as single cells was significantly reduced compared with that of control iPSC-NCCs (WD39).
source: A comparison of two different cell lines, WD39 and CH2#16 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B) yielded similar results; the average velocity of CHARGE iPSC-NCCs migrating as single cells was significantly reduced compared with that of control iPSC-NCCs (Sidak's multiple comparisons test after two-way repeated measures ANOVA: pTime <0.001, pCellType <0.001; WD39, N = 170 cells tracked; CH2#16, N = 133 cells tracked).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse tracking data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The abnormal migration of CHARGE iPSC-NCCs is due, at least in part, to a defective intrinsic motility.
source: In contrast, the directionality of CHARGE iPSC-NCCs was not different to that of control iPSC-NCCs, indicating that the abnormal migration of CHARGE iPSC-NCCs is due, at least in part, to a defective intrinsic motility.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that velocity is reduced but directionality is preserved in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs.

claim: Both control and CHARGE iPSC-NCCs migrated in the expected direction, consistent with the normal developmental routes of NCCs in chick embryos.
source: Both control and CHARGE iPSC-NCCs migrated in the expected direction, consistent with the normal developmental routes of NCCs.
evidence: This is observed from the in ovo transplantation experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: CHARGE iPSC-NCCs did not follow abnormal routes to ectopic sites in the chick embryo model.
source: Notably, CHARGE iPSC-NCCs did not follow abnormal routes to ectopic sites in this model.
evidence: This is observed from the in ovo transplantation experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: CHARGE iPSC-NCCs exhibited similar or lower migration scores compared with those of the co-transplanted control iPSC-NCCs in chick embryos.
source: As shown in Figure 7C, CHARGE iPSC-NCCs exhibited similar or lower migration scores compared with those of the co-transplanted control iPSC-NCCs.
evidence: This is supported by migration scoring data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In 6 of 9 transplanted embryos, the velocity of CHARGE iPSC-NCCs was significantly less than that of control cells.
source: In 6 of 9 transplanted embryos, the velocity of CHARGE iPSC-NCCs was significantly less than that of control cells.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse tracking data from in ovo experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Collectively, CHARGE iPSC-NCCs exhibited a lower velocity compared with that of the co-transplanted control iPSC-NCCs in chick embryos.
source: Collectively, CHARGE iPSC-NCCs exhibited a lower velocity compared with that of the co-transplanted control iPSC-NCCs (p=0.03; Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of velocity data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The reduced migratory capability of CHARGE iPSC-NCCs observed in vitro reflects their reduced migration in vivo after transplantation in chick embryo.
source: These data suggest that the reduced migratory capability of CHARGE iPSC-NCCs observed in vitro reflects their reduced migration in vivo after transplantation in chick embryo.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency between in vitro and in vivo migration defects.

claim: It was previously shown by CHD7 knockdown in human ESCs that CHD7 controls EMT in multipotent NCCs.
source: It was previously shown by CHD7 knockdown in human ESCs that CHD7 controls EMT in multipotent NCCs (Bajpai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the citation of Bajpai et al., 2010.

claim: CHARGE iPSC-NCCs have migratory defects and a series of migration-related behaviors following EMT, namely, delamination, migration, and motility, are affected.
source: Our results using CHARGE syndrome patient-derived iPSCs indicate that CHARGE iPSC-NCCs have migratory defects and that a series of migration-related behaviors following EMT, namely, delamination, migration, and motility, are affected.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from Figures 4-7.

claim: FOXD1 expression was upregulated in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs.
source: As shown in Figure 3E, FOXD1 expression was upregulated in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: FOXD1 is known to be expressed in premigratory NCCs and extinguished once migration occurs.
source: Since FOXD1 is known to be expressed in premigratory NCCs and extinguished once migration occurs (Gómez-Skarmeta et al., 1999), altered FOXD1 expression may lead to a defective premigratory-to-migratory transition occurring in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs.
evidence: This is supported by the citation of Gómez-Skarmeta et al., 1999.

claim: Altered FOXD1 expression may lead to a defective premigratory-to-migratory transition occurring in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs.
source: Since FOXD1 is known to be expressed in premigratory NCCs and extinguished once migration occurs (Gómez-Skarmeta et al., 1999), altered FOXD1 expression may lead to a defective premigratory-to-migratory transition occurring in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on known FOXD1 function and observed upregulation in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs.

claim: All cranial NCCs are suggested to have similar migratory potential, unlike trunk NCCs, which are known to be a heterozygous population consisting of cells such as leader cells and follower cells.
source: All cranial NCCs are suggested to have similar migratory potential, unlike trunk NCCs, which are known to be a heterozygous population consisting of cells such as leader cells and follower cells (Richardson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the citation of Richardson et al., 2016.

claim: The expression levels of POU3F2 (BRN2) and OLFM3 (Optimedin) were significantly downregulated in CHARGE compared with control iPSC-NCCs.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, the expression levels of POU3F2 (BRN2) and OLFM3 (Optimedin) were significantly downregulated in CHARGE compared with control iPSC-NCCs, and these two genes have been reported to be targets of PAX6 (Grinchuk et al., 2005) (Ninkovic et al., 2013) (Raviv et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: POU3F2 and OLFM3 have been reported to be targets of PAX6.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, the expression levels of POU3F2 (BRN2) and OLFM3 (Optimedin) were significantly downregulated in CHARGE compared with control iPSC-NCCs, and these two genes have been reported to be targets of PAX6 (Grinchuk et al., 2005) (Ninkovic et al., 2013) (Raviv et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations: Grinchuk et al., 2005; Ninkovic et al., 2013; Raviv et al., 2014.

claim: POU3F2 is involved in controlling the migration of melanocytes, which are neural crest derivatives.
source: POU3F2 is involved in controlling the migration of melanocytes, which are neural crest derivatives (Berlin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the citation of Berlin et al., 2012.

claim: OLFM3 is considered to be involved in cell-cell adhesion and cell attachment to the extracellular matrix.
source: OLFM3 is considered to be involved in cell-cell adhesion and cell attachment to the extracellular matrix (Grinchuk et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the citation of Grinchuk et al., 2005.

claim: Several downstream targets of Pax6 have been identified as cell adhesion molecules and structural proteins.
source: Several downstream targets of Pax6 have been identified as cell adhesion molecules and structural proteins (Cvekl and Callaerts, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the citation of Cvekl and Callaerts, 2017.

claim: Altered CHD7 expression resulted in the upregulation of PAX6 and the downregulation of PAX6 downstream genes.
source: Altered CHD7 expression resulted in the upregulation of PAX6 and the downregulation of PAX6 downstream genes (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: It is conceivable that CHD7 regulates multipotent NCC migration by cooperating with PAX6.
source: Therefore, it is conceivable that CHD7 regulates multipotent NCC migration by cooperating with PAX6.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed gene expression changes and known functions of CHD7 and PAX6.

claim: CTGF and EDN1, known to be downstream factors in the Hippo-YAP signaling pathway, are highly expressed in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs compared with control cells.
source: Next, CTGF and EDN1, known to be downstream factors in the Hippo-YAP signaling pathway, are highly expressed in CHARGE iPSC-NCCs compared with control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.
